catholics-worship-mary.summary: The Church teaches that worship belongs to God alone: Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Mary is honoured as the Mother of God, and Catholics ask her to pray for them. The Church says this honour is a different kind from the worship we give to God.

steps.0: The Catechism says devotion to Mary is real. It is different from worship of God.
steps.1: The first commandment says worship is owed to God alone.
steps.2: Even an angel in Revelation refuses worship and points to God.
steps.3: Ambrose says plainly that Mary is not to be worshipped.
steps.4: Augustine names the difference: one kind of worship is for God only.
steps.5: Cyril says Mary is the mother of God because her Son is God.
steps.6: In the Magnificat Mary gives all the glory to God.
steps.7: In the Hail Mary, Catholics ask Mary to pray for them.

objections: Kneeling and praying can mean different things. In the Hail Mary we ask Mary to “pray for us”. Christians ask each other for prayer in the same way. Titles like Queen honour her place. They do not make her God.
Sometimes that does happen. The Church does not defend it. Honouring a creature in place of God is idolatry. A person who does it is going against the Church’s teaching.

catholics-worship-statues.summary: The Church condemns idolatry. Catholics do not worship statues as things. A statue or icon is honoured because of the person it shows. The honour passes to that person. Only God is adored.

steps.0: The Church keeps the Old Testament ban on idols.
steps.1: The commandment bans making idols to worship them. The Church takes it seriously.
steps.2: God himself orders carved golden cherubim for the ark.
steps.3: God has Moses make a bronze serpent for healing. The healing came from God.
steps.4: The Second Council of Nicaea allowed honour to images, not worship.
steps.5: The Catechism says honour goes through the image to the person.
steps.6: Trent repeated the rule and told bishops to remove superstition.

objections: The same God who gave that commandment ordered the cherubim and the bronze serpent. Christians also believe that when God took a human face in Christ, things changed.
Some did, and it was a real debate. Clement of Alexandria wrote against images in the setting of pagan temples. The Church worked it out over centuries.

church-banned-the-bible.summary: The Church copied, kept, translated and read the Bible aloud from the start. Today she urges every Catholic to read it. At some times and places, church leaders did limit lay people owning the Bible and unapproved translations. That part of the story should be told honestly.

steps.0: The Church today says Scripture should be open to all the faithful.
steps.1: The Church urges all Christians to read the Bible often. Not knowing it is not knowing Christ.
steps.2: All Scripture is useful. It is for the whole people of God.
steps.3: Chrysostom tells ordinary married people to read Scripture.
steps.4: Augustine’s conversion came when he picked up Paul’s letter.
steps.5: Many Latin translations existed in Augustine’s day, so ordinary people could read them.

objections: In some places and times, yes. In 1229 a council at Toulouse, dealing with groups in southern France, forbade lay people to own the books of Scripture, apart from a Psalter and a few others. That was a real restriction, and the Church does not hide it.
Latin was the everyday language in the western Roman world about the year 400, when Jerome translated the Bible. Later, Latin lasted longer than the languages people spoke, and a gap grew.

catholics-pray-to-the-dead.summary: The Church forbids necromancy, which means trying to call up the dead. Catholics ask the saints in heaven to pray for them. The saints are alive in Christ. It is like asking a friend on earth to pray. Christians do disagree about this.

steps.0: The Catechism says the saints share in the Church’s prayer. We ask them to pray for us.
steps.1: The Church forbids calling up the dead.
steps.2: The Bible bans asking the dead for secret knowledge or power.
steps.3: Jesus says Abraham, Isaac and Jacob are alive to God.
steps.4: In heaven the elders offer the prayers of the saints.
steps.5: In a vision, two dead holy men pray for Israel.
steps.6: Ambrose advises Christians to ask the martyrs to pray for them.
steps.7: Augustine says Christians honour the martyrs and do not treat them as gods.

objections: In the same passage Paul tells Christians to pray for all people. So he does not mean no one else may pray. Christ is the one Mediator who brings us to the Father. The saints pray in him.

Catholics believe the saints are alive in Christ, with God. They are not wandering spirits to question. We do not give them orders or ask about the future. We ask for their prayers, as we would ask a friend.

pope-claims-to-be-sinless.summary: No. The Church teaches that the pope is kept from error when he solemnly teaches the whole Church a point of faith or morals. That is called infallibility. It has nothing to do with being without sin. Popes go to confession like everyone else.

steps.0: The Catechism says what is claimed: the pope is protected from error when he defines a doctrine.
steps.1: Even this gift is limited. It does not make him inspired or sinless.
steps.2: Jesus prays for Peter’s faith. Peter will fall and turn back.
steps.3: The first pope calls himself a sinner.
steps.4: Paul corrects Peter in public. The first pope could sin.
steps.5: The Catechism says the Church’s ministers, popes too, are sinners who need conversion.
steps.6: Pope Gregory the Great called himself a grievous sinner.

objections: Only in a narrow way. It covers the pope teaching the whole Church on faith or morals in a solemn act. It does not cover his private opinions.

It disproves a claim the Church does not make. The Church has never said popes are sinless. Some popes lived badly, and the Church does not hide that. She says Christ keeps his promise to protect the faith.

catholics-believe-works-earn-salvation.summary: The Church teaches that salvation starts and ends with God’s free grace. Good works are the fruit of that grace. Nothing we do before we are justified earns it.

steps.0: The Catechism starts with grace, free and undeserved.
steps.1: No one can earn the very first grace.
steps.2: Paul says salvation is a gift. Catholics hold this firmly.
steps.3: The same passage says God prepared good works for us.
steps.4: Augustine treats the idea that we earn grace as a mistake.
steps.5: Trent rejects being justified by one’s own works without grace.
steps.6: Trent says neither faith nor works earns the first grace.
steps.7: Trent says merit is God crowning his own gifts.

objections: Paul and James speak of different things. Paul speaks of works before faith. James speaks of a faith that is alive. The Church says we cooperate with grace, and even that is grace at work.
Merit means God, by his promise, lets our graced acts count toward a reward. The Catechism says we have no strict right to merit from God. We received everything from him.

eucharist-just-a-symbol.summary: From the New Testament on, Christians took Jesus’ words “This is my body” to mean the Eucharist is truly his body and blood. The Church writers also call it a sign. But they also call it the real flesh of Christ. The Church uses the same words.

steps.0: The Catechism states it plainly: Christ is truly present.
steps.1: Jesus insists on eating his flesh and does not soften it.
steps.2: Paul calls the bread a real sharing in Christ’s body.
steps.3: Paul says whoever eats unworthily is guilty of the body and blood of the Lord.
steps.4: Ignatius calls the bread of God the flesh of Christ.
steps.5: Irenaeus says the bread and wine become Christ’s body, and uses this to prove his flesh is real.
steps.6: Ambrose says the altar holds the same flesh that was crucified.
steps.7: Chrysostom says to believe Christ’s words over what the senses say.
steps.8: John of Damascus sums up the teaching of the East.

objections: Yes. The Church uses the same words because a sacrament is a sign. Some readers take Augustine as purely symbolic, and scholars still talk about it. The Church reads him in the light of the rest of what he wrote.
The word is from the Middle Ages. Trent used it to define the change exactly. The belief behind it, that the bread and wine become Christ’s body and blood, is much older.

catholics-add-books-to-the-bible.summary: Catholic Bibles have seven Old Testament books that Protestant Bibles leave out. They are Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch, and 1 and 2 Maccabees. Christians read them in the Greek Old Testament long before the Reformation. Protestants removed them in the sixteenth century.

steps.0: The Church sees the canon as received, not made up.
steps.1: The New Testament seems to refer to the story in 2 Maccabees 7.
steps.2: Hippolytus reads Maccabees as a trusted history.
steps.3: Origen says the book is not in the Hebrew copies, and the Churches use it anyway.
steps.4: Ambrose quotes 2 Maccabees as Scripture.
steps.5: Augustine’s list, long before Trent, includes these books.
steps.6: Trent lists the books the Church receives. It confirmed what the Church already used.

objections: That is a fair point, and Christians have long known it. Augustine said the Jews are said not to have received Judith. But the Church of the apostles used the Greek translation, which had these books.
The first formal definition for all by a council was at Trent. But lists like the Catholic one were in use in the 300s and 400s, as in Augustine’s list.

purgatory-invented-to-make-money.summary: Purgatory is the Church’s name for the last cleansing of people who die in God’s friendship but are not yet fully holy. It has roots in the Bible and in the old Christian habit of praying for the dead. The word and the details came later. Selling indulgences did cause real abuses.

steps.0: The Catechism calls it the last step for those already saved. It is not a second chance.
steps.1: Judas Maccabeus offers a sacrifice for the dead long before Christ.
steps.2: Paul speaks of a person saved “as through fire”.
steps.3: Chrysostom tells people to help their dead with prayer and gifts.
steps.4: Monica asks only to be remembered at the altar.
steps.5: Augustine describes in outline what the Church later named.
steps.6: Trent states the teaching. It also tells bishops to stop anything that looks like greed.

objections: The word came later, as the Catechism says. It was set out at later councils. The early writers do not agree on every detail. The practice of praying for the dead is old.
Yes. In the late Middle Ages money was tied to indulgences in shocking ways. The Church later admitted it. Trent ended money-making in connection with indulgences.

priests-forgive-sins-instead-of-god.summary: The Church teaches that only God forgives sins. In the sacrament of Penance, Christ gives forgiveness through bishops and priests. They act in his name, as he promised the apostles.

steps.0: The Catechism starts with “Only God forgives sins”.
steps.1: The scribes ask who can forgive but God. Jesus claims that power.
steps.2: The crowd praises God for giving such power to people.
steps.3: On Easter night Jesus gives the apostles this power.
steps.4: Paul calls the apostles ambassadors of reconciliation.
steps.5: Cyprian says Christians confessed even troubled thoughts to priests.
steps.6: Ambrose says refusing the power Christ gave is itself wrong.
steps.7: Trent says the priest gives a gift that is God’s.

objections: Catholics also talk to God. The Church teaches that sorrow out of love for God brings forgiveness, if the person means to go to Confession. The sacrament is the normal way Christ gave.
Yes. In the early centuries serious sins were often confessed and made up for in public. Private confession grew slowly. By the third and fourth centuries, writers like Cyprian and Ambrose show it.

church-opposed-science-galileo.summary: The Church teaches that faith and reason cannot truly contradict, because one God is the source of both. The Galileo case was a real failure by Church officials. But it was not a Catholic teaching, and it does not show the Church is against science.

steps.0: The Catechism says one God is the source of faith and nature.
steps.1: Augustine said long ago to welcome truth from any source.
steps.2: Some verses speak as an observer on the ground would. Some people took them literally.
steps.3: The Church asks what the writer was really saying.
steps.4: A council says such clashes come from misreading faith or taking an opinion as fact.
steps.5: A pope says new discoveries about nature do not draw Church opposition.
steps.6: The Catechism says studying the cosmos is a reason to praise the Creator.

objections: The condemnation happened and it was a mistake. The Church has said so. It was a judgment by a Roman court, not a defined teaching of the faith.

The Church holds that Scripture teaches the truths God revealed for our salvation. She asks how an author is speaking. We still say “sunrise” and “sunset” today. Reading those words as a science lesson is a mistake.

church-young-earth-rejects-evolution.summary: The Church has never fixed the age of the earth. The Catechism welcomes the scientific study of the universe and of life. The Church holds to things science cannot measure. God made everything. Every human soul is made directly by God. The fall of the first humans was a real event.

steps.0: The Catechism speaks warmly of research into the age of the cosmos and of life.
steps.1: The “when and how” belongs to science. The Church cares about meaning.
steps.2: The Catechism calls the six days a symbolic way of speaking.
steps.3: Genesis 1–3 teaches truths about God, the world and people, in solemn language.
steps.4: Genesis says God is the Creator of all.
steps.5: Augustine said the six days did not mean six stretches of time.
steps.6: Augustine did count under six thousand years from Adam, using the dates he had.
steps.7: Whatever the body’s history, each soul comes directly from God.

objections: Some did, as a rough count from the family lists of their time. A Father’s date guess is not Church teaching. Augustine read the “days” differently.
The Catechism does not rule on how living things changed. It leaves that to science. The Church holds that God made the world, that it is not blind chance, and that each soul is made directly by God.

celibacy-invented-middle-ages.summary: In the Latin Church, priests staying unmarried is a rule the Church can change. It is not a doctrine of the faith. It rests on Christ’s praise of those who give up marriage for the Kingdom. Eastern Catholic Churches ordain married men.

steps.0: The Latin Church’s rule is stated as normal practice. Permanent deacons are an exception.
steps.1: Other Catholic traditions ordain married men, so it is a rule and not a doctrine.
steps.2: Christ speaks of those who give up marriage for the Kingdom. He calls it a gift.
steps.3: Paul gives the reason: an undivided heart for the Lord.
steps.4: Some apostles, Peter among them, were married.
steps.5: Jerome honoured celibacy and did not condemn marriage.
steps.6: A council about 305 already asked married clergy to abstain.
steps.7: Trent says the duty rests on Church law or a vow.

objections: It shows that married men were bishops in the first generation. The Church admits that. Chrysostom read it as a limit on remarriage, not a command to marry.
The Church sees it as a fitting sign of the Kingdom. It lets a priest give himself fully to God and to people. It is a gift and not for every man.

trinity-word-not-in-the-bible.summary: The word “Trinity” is not in the Bible. The truth it names is. Father, Son and Holy Spirit are named together as one God from the time of the apostles. The Church made the word to guard what the Bible says when other readings came up.

steps.0: One name and three Persons, in the words of baptism.
steps.1: A blessing names Father, Son and Spirit side by side.
steps.2: Paul names Spirit, Lord and God as one source of all in the Church.
steps.3: Tertullian is one of the first to use the word.
steps.4: Origen speaks of the Trinity in a Latin translation, which may have changed some words.
steps.5: Nicaea uses careful words to guard what the Bible says about the Son.
steps.6: The Catechism says the teaching grew from baptism faith.
steps.7: The Catechism says the words are the Church’s own, made to express what was given.

objections: The Church has always held that Scripture and the apostles’ Tradition come from one source. The Church that gathered the New Testament is also trusted to explain it.
In part, yes. The Church used words like “substance” and “person”, as the Catechism says. The word “homoousios” is not in the Bible. The aim was to say what was already believed.

constantine-invented-christ-divinity.summary: Christians worshipped Jesus as God long before Constantine. The New Testament itself calls him God. At Nicaea in 325 the bishops did not make up the belief. They answered Arius, who said the Son was not eternally God, and they put the faith in exact words.

steps.0: John opens by calling the Word God, over two hundred years earlier.
steps.1: Thomas calls Jesus God and Jesus accepts it.
steps.2: An early hymn says Christ was in the form of God before he became man.
steps.3: Ignatius, long before Nicaea, calls Jesus Christ “our God”.
steps.4: Justin argues that Christ is God, as an ordinary Christian view.
steps.5: The Nicene Creed states in exact words what Christians already believed.
steps.6: Eusebius reports that the emperor welcomed the key word. This should be admitted.
steps.7: The Catechism sees Nicaea as the confession of an existing faith.

objections: The council began because of Arius, who said there was a time when the Son was not. The bishops rejected that and wrote the creed. They were not deciding whether to begin calling Jesus God.
Constantine called the council and was there. Later emperors also interfered, sometimes for the Arian side. Politics cut both ways. The teaching did not depend on one emperor.

saved-by-baptism-alone.summary: The Church teaches that baptism is needed for salvation. It is a true beginning of new life, not a guarantee. Faith has to grow and show itself in love. A baptized person can lose grace by grave sin.

steps.0: The Church teaches baptism is necessary, with limits she herself states.
steps.1: The Gospel puts belief and baptism together.
steps.2: Paul says God saves us through the washing of baptism, as a gift of mercy.
steps.3: Baptism is where Christian life starts, not where it ends.
steps.4: Jesus says words are not enough without doing the Father’s will.
steps.5: Paul sums up: a living faith that acts in love.
steps.6: Trent says faith without works is dead.
steps.7: Baptism leaves a mark, but sin can stop it from bearing fruit.

objections: No. Baptism gives a baby new life with God. The child must grow in faith. The Church teaches that faith without works is dead, and that sin can separate even a baptized person from Christ.
The Church teaches that God is not tied to his sacraments. A catechumen who dies before baptism, a martyr, and a person who sincerely seeks God without knowing the Gospel can all be saved.

non-catholics-cannot-be-saved.summary: The Church teaches that all salvation comes from Christ through the Church, which is his Body. She does not teach that everyone outside her visible limits is lost. People who do not know Christ or his Church through no fault of their own, and who sincerely seek God, can be saved.

steps.0: The old phrase is about people who know and still refuse.
steps.1: The Catechism says salvation is not closed to people who sincerely seek God without knowing Christ.
steps.2: Baptized Protestant and Orthodox Christians are not outsiders to Christ.
steps.3: All salvation is through Christ alone.
steps.4: Peter sees that God accepts those who seek him sincerely.
steps.5: Paul says God judges by the law written on hearts.
steps.6: Justin taught that the Word is present in every human mind.
steps.7: Cyprian wrote the strict form against Christians who knowingly broke from the Church.

objections: The words are the same. The explanation has been made clearer. The Church should admit that some later statements were stricter than Cyprian. He was speaking to baptized Christians who had cut themselves off.

The Church holds that Christ and the fullness of the means of grace are given in her. No one should be kept from them. Hope for those who have not heard is left to God’s mercy. It is not a reason to stop sharing the Gospel.

catholics-worship-the-pope.summary: No. Catholics worship God alone: Father, Son and Holy Spirit. The pope is honoured as Peter’s successor and the visible centre of the Church’s unity. His authority serves the faith. It cannot add to it.

steps.0: Worship is for God alone as Creator and Saviour.
steps.1: Jesus says to worship the Lord God and serve him only.
steps.2: Peter refuses worship from Cornelius. Catholics see this as the model for popes.
steps.3: The pope’s office is about unity and care of the flock.
steps.4: Vatican I limits infallibility to guarding what was revealed. The pope cannot invent new teaching.
steps.5: Infallibility covers solemn teaching on faith or morals, not his opinions.
steps.6: Gregory the Great called himself servant of the servants of God.

objections: Kneeling and kissing a ring are signs of respect for his office. The Church separates honour for holy people and things from worship of God. Peter refused to be worshipped by Cornelius.

The title means the pope acts for Christ, as Peter was given the keys. He does not replace Christ. Infallibility is a narrow gift to guard the Church’s teaching. It does not make him perfect. Popes go to confession.

sunday-worship-invented-by-the-church.summary: The New Testament shows the first Christians meeting on the first day of the week, the day of the Resurrection. The Church has kept Sunday as the Lord’s Day since the time of the apostles. The Bible has no clear command to move the Sabbath. The Church says Sunday comes from apostolic Tradition and from Christ’s rising.

steps.0: The risen Jesus appears to his disciples on the first day of the week.
steps.1: Luke tells of a first-day gathering to break bread.
steps.2: Paul expects a weekly first-day gathering.
steps.3: Most readers take “the Lord’s day” to mean Sunday.
steps.4: Paul says not to judge people over the Sabbath. It is a shadow now fulfilled in Christ.
steps.5: Justin describes Christian worship in Rome on Sunday.
steps.6: Origen takes the Lord’s day for granted.
steps.7: Nicaea treats praying on the Lord’s days as settled practice.
steps.8: The Catechism says Sunday fulfills the Sabbath. It does not drop the idea of a holy day.

objections: Constantine’s law in 321 made Sunday a day of rest. It was added to something already kept. The New Testament shows first-day meetings over two hundred years earlier.
The Church says Christ rose on the first day, and the apostles made that the new centre of worship. The Sabbath is not cancelled. Its deepest meaning, rest in God, is fulfilled in Christ.

catholics-dont-read-the-bible.summary: The Church urges every Catholic to read the Bible often. The Mass is built from it. Many Catholics may not read it as much as they should. That is a failure of habit, not a failure of teaching.

steps.0: The Catechism urges every Catholic to read Scripture often.
steps.1: The Bible must be open to all the faithful.
steps.2: Every Mass is built from Scripture.
steps.3: All Scripture is God’s word and useful for every Christian.
steps.4: Augustine’s conversion came from reading Scripture.
steps.5: Jerome urged constant reading.
steps.6: Chrysostom told ordinary people to get Bibles for home.
steps.7: A pope compares the Bible to a letter from God, to be read daily.

objections: In some times and places it was hard to get a Bible. There was cost, no printing, and rules against unapproved translations. Those rules were real. They do not match what the early Fathers taught.
It may say something true about habits, and the Church would not deny it. But the Church teaches the opposite of keeping Catholics from the Bible.

mary-sinless-romans-3-23.summary: The Church teaches that Mary was saved by Christ like everyone else, but in a special way. She was kept free from original sin from the first moment of her life, because of what her Son would do. By God’s grace she stayed free from personal sin. Paul’s “all have sinned” is a general statement.

steps.0: The Catechism says Mary was redeemed. She is not outside salvation.
steps.1: Her holiness comes wholly from Christ.
steps.2: The 1854 definition says this was because of the merits of Christ.
steps.3: Gabriel greets Mary with a title, “highly favored”.
steps.4: Mary herself calls God her Saviour.
steps.5: Romans 3:23 speaks of humanity as a whole.
steps.6: Augustine makes a careful exception for Mary when he speaks of sin.

objections: The Church says she needed Christ’s work fully, and received its fruit early. The Catechism calls her the most excellent fruit of redemption. Stopping a fall is also a kind of rescue.
It was defined in 1854. Honest history adds that great teachers like Aquinas and Bernard hesitated over it. It was debated for centuries before the argument that settled it.

confess-to-priest-small-sins.summary: The Church requires Confession for serious sin. For everyday faults she recommends it but does not require it. Small, or venial, sins can be forgiven in other ways: prayer, the Eucharist, and acts of love and sorrow.

steps.0: Mortal sin breaks friendship with God. Venial sin wounds it.
steps.1: Serious sins a person knows about must be confessed to a priest.
steps.2: The Catechism says confessing small sins is not strictly needed, but it is recommended.
steps.3: Trent says venial sins may be left out without guilt.
steps.4: The Eucharist is one of the other remedies for everyday faults.
steps.5: Augustine says the Lord’s Prayer takes care of the small sins of each day.
steps.6: The risen Christ gives the apostles a real ministry of forgiving sins.

objections: The Church agrees only God forgives. Sorrow out of love for God wins forgiveness even before Confession. But Christ also gave a visible way, and a person aware of serious sin must use it.
Many Catholics have felt that way, and some were taught so. It has caused real worry. The teaching is gentler. Small sins do not cut a person off from God.

church-treats-women-lesser.summary: The Church teaches that men and women have the same dignity, as people made in God’s image. She holds up a woman, Mary, as the greatest of all creatures. She also teaches that only baptized men can be priests. She says this is about Christ’s choice of the Twelve, not about the worth of women.

steps.0: Man and woman have equal dignity, directly from God.
steps.1: In Christ and in baptism, women stand fully equal with men.
steps.2: A woman is the first sent to tell the apostles about the Resurrection.
steps.3: Paul commends Phoebe and Prisca for their work in the Church.
steps.4: Holiness comes before office. The greatest example is a woman.
steps.5: Macrina taught her brothers Basil and Gregory of Nyssa.
steps.6: The Church says she is bound by Christ’s own choice of men.

objections: The Church says priesthood is a service, not a prize. No one has a right to it, not even men. She also says the highest human being, Mary, was not a priest. Many people do not find this convincing. The Church states it plainly.

It is true some old writers, saints too, wrote about women in ways the Church would not repeat today. Tertullian called women “the devil’s gateway”. Aquinas followed Aristotle in views the Church no longer holds.

transubstantiation-magical-thinking.summary: The Church teaches that at the consecration the whole substance of the bread and wine changes into the Body and Blood of Christ. The looks stay the same. She does not say this can be seen or tested. She says we receive it on Christ’s word. It is God’s work, not a spell by the priest.

steps.0: The word “transubstantiation” names the change.
steps.1: Trent says what stays is the appearance.
steps.2: Aquinas says this is a matter of faith in Christ’s word, not the senses.
steps.3: The doctrine rests on “This is my body”.
steps.4: Jesus says his flesh is “food indeed”.
steps.5: Cyril of Jerusalem taught about 350 that the bread becomes Christ’s body.
steps.6: Ambrose says that if a prophet’s word could change things, Christ’s word can too.

objections: That is right, and the Church agrees. She does not call it a science claim. It is a mystery that rests on Christ’s word. Whether that is a good reason to believe is a fair question.

Many sincere Christians read it that way. Catholics do not call that foolish. They answer that early Christians spoke of the Eucharist as truly the Body and Blood, and Jesus did not soften the hard saying in John 6.

divorce-forbidden-annulment.summary: The Church does not forbid divorce out of cruelty. Following Jesus, she teaches that a valid marriage between baptized people, once complete, cannot be ended by any human power. She allows couples to separate. She accepts civil divorce when it is needed. She can also declare that a marriage was never valid in the first place.

steps.0: Jesus points back to creation: what God has joined, let no one tear apart.
steps.1: The Catechism says God makes the bond. The Church has no power to undo it.
steps.2: Augustine, about 401, already taught marriage is a lasting bond with a holy character.
steps.3: Trent grounds the teaching in Genesis and Christ. It allows separation for many reasons.
steps.4: The Church does not ask a spouse to stay in danger.
steps.5: The Catechism treats the innocent person in a divorce differently from the one who caused it.
steps.6: A marriage exists only by free consent. Without it, there was no marriage.
steps.7: An annulment is a finding about the past. It does not end a marriage.

objections: The Church is open to this worry. Church courts are run by people. Many Catholics found the process slow, confusing or painful. Church leaders have called for reform. What the Church says is that an annulment is a finding, not a divorce.
The Church does not say that. Spouses can separate. The bond remains, but that is different from having to stay in danger. The Church hopes for peace where it is possible.

catholics-not-allowed-to-think.summary: The Church teaches that faith and reason come from the same God and cannot truly clash. Believers are meant to look for understanding. She also holds that some teachings are definite, and a Catholic cannot simply deny them. In history she has sometimes limited inquiry in ways she later regretted.

steps.0: Faith and reason cannot really be opposed. Honest research cannot clash with faith.
steps.1: Wanting to understand more is part of faith.
steps.2: Faith is not meant to be blind. It rests on signs and reasons.
steps.3: The Bereans are praised for checking even Paul’s preaching.
steps.4: Paul says to test everything and hold on to what is good.
steps.5: Anselm gives the famous phrase: faith looking for understanding.
steps.6: Vatican I says reason is a gift to use.

objections: The Church holds some teachings as binding. A Catholic who denies them is not in full agreement with the faith. But the Church separates doubt and difficulty from denial. A person may have many questions.
Yes. The Index of Forbidden Books was a real system that limited reading. People were tried for their ideas. Galileo is the best known. In 1992 Pope John Paul II admitted mistakes in that case.

hell-medieval-scare-tactic.summary: The teaching on hell does not come from the Middle Ages. It is in the preaching of Jesus and in the earliest Fathers. The Church teaches that hell is a lasting choice to shut God out. God chooses no one for hell. The warnings are a call to freedom and to turn back.

steps.0: Hell is a free choice that is not reversed, not an order from outside.
steps.1: God sends no one to hell by decree. It takes a deliberate, lasting refusal.
steps.2: The warning is Jesus’ own, about failing to feed, welcome and visit the poor.
steps.3: God wants all to be saved.
steps.4: Justin, about 155, already speaks of eternal fire.
steps.5: Augustine rejects the idea that baptized people who stay in grave sin are surely saved.
steps.6: The Catechism says these teachings are a call to responsibility and turning back.

objections: There is truth in this. Much of the vivid imagery in preaching and art comes from later centuries. The Catechism puts the weight elsewhere. The chief punishment is being apart from God.

This question has troubled Christians a lot. The Church does not claim to know that anyone is in hell. She teaches that it is possible because love cannot be forced. The Church prays that no one is lost.

suffering-is-gods-punishment.summary: The Church does not teach that a person’s suffering is a punishment for that person’s sin. She teaches that suffering and death came into the world through sin in general. God does not will evil but can bring good from it. In Christ, suffering can be joined to his own.

steps.0: God does not cause evil. He allows it because of human freedom, and can bring good from it.
steps.1: Israel saw a link between sickness and sin. The Catechism says the mystery of suffering is deeper.
steps.2: Jesus rejects the link between a man’s blindness and his sin.
steps.3: Jesus says the victims of a tower falling were not worse sinners.
steps.4: God says Job’s friends were wrong.
steps.5: Augustine says the blind man’s parents were sinners like everyone, and still this was not the cause.
steps.6: Christ took on suffering and gave it new meaning.
steps.7: Paul calls God the one who comforts those in trouble.

objections: The two are related, but not as the claim says. The Catechism speaks of “temporal punishment” as the leftover damage sin leaves. Christians can accept suffering as a grace. It does not mean each pain is a punishment.

The Church says suffering joined to Christ can have meaning, as Paul says. She does not say the sufferer earned it. The phrase has sometimes been said carelessly and has hurt people. That should be admitted.

indulgences-buy-your-way-out.summary: An indulgence is not forgiveness of sin, and it cannot be bought. It removes the leftover damage that remains after a sin is forgiven. It needs the person’s own turning back. In the 1500s, money was wrongly tied to indulgences, with some campaigns approved by the pope. The Church later ended this.

steps.0: An indulgence is about sins already forgiven. It cannot forgive guilt.
steps.1: “Temporal punishment” means the healing still needed after forgiveness.
steps.2: An indulgence asks something of the person, in prayer, penance or love.
steps.3: The Church claims authority from Christ’s power of binding and loosing.
steps.4: Cyprian, about 250, describes lapsed Christians helped by martyrs, but only after confessing.
steps.5: Scripture condemns trying to buy a spiritual gift. The Church later named this simony.
steps.6: In 1563 Trent admitted abuses and ordered the money-making to stop.

objections: Yes. Money was tied to indulgences in a way that made many think forgiveness could be bought. The Church had to admit it was an abuse. Trent ended the money-making.

The Church says sin leaves damage, and healing takes time, like a wound after the cause is removed. People may or may not find that reasonable. It is different from the claim that forgiveness is for sale.

early-christians-no-bishops-or-priests.summary: The New Testament already shows chosen leaders: overseers, elders and deacons, named by laying on of hands. About the year 107 Ignatius describes each church with a bishop, elders and deacons. About 180 Irenaeus lists bishops back to the apostles. The Church holds that these three ministries go back to the beginning.

steps.0: The Catechism says the three ministries have existed from the beginning.
steps.1: About 60, Paul writes to Philippi’s overseers and servants.
steps.2: Paul and Barnabas appoint elders in every community.
steps.3: Timothy received a gift through the laying on of hands.
steps.4: About 107, Ignatius takes for granted a bishop in each church.
steps.5: About 180, Irenaeus points to lists of bishops back to the apostles.
steps.6: Trent says this threefold shape comes from Christ.

objections: Yes, in places the two words seem to mean the same office. The Church does not hide that. Jerome noticed it too. The Church says the offices existed and titles settled over time.

The Church agrees that all baptized people share in Christ’s priesthood. She adds that Scripture also shows some chosen to lead and serve. The Catechism says the two are ordered to one another, but are not the same.
